read.sections.0.heading.source: A map shows a place from above

read.sections.0.text.note: 'Babylon' written as 'Babilonia'; 'charts' as 'peta'; 'clay tablet' as 'lempeng tanah liat'.
read.sections.0.text.back: A map is a picture of a place, usually as a bird sees it from the sky. A map cannot show everything, so the map-maker chooses what to put in. For example, a bus map shows bus stops, and a rain map shows the places that have the most rain. Humans have made maps for thousands of years. About 2,500 years ago, someone in the region that is now Iraq made a world map on a clay tablet. That map shows the city of Babylon in the middle. In the Marshall Islands in the Pacific Ocean, sailors made maps from sticks and shells. The sticks showed the movement of ocean waves, and the shells showed the islands.
read.sections.0.text.source: A map is a drawing of a place, usually as a bird would see it from the sky. A map cannot show everything, so the mapmaker chooses what to include. For example, a bus map shows bus stops, and a rain map shows where it rains most. People have made maps for thousands of years. About 2,500 years ago, someone in today's Iraq made a map of the world on a clay tablet. It shows the city of Babylon in the middle. In the Marshall Islands in the Pacific Ocean, sailors made charts from sticks and shells. The sticks showed how ocean waves moved, and the shells showed islands.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: A map is a picture of a place. A map shows that place from above, as a bird sees it. A map cannot show everything. The map-maker chooses what to show. A bus map shows bus stops. People in the old days also made maps. Someone in the area that is now Iraq made a map from clay. Sailors in the Marshall Islands made maps from sticks and shells. The shells show islands.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: A map is a picture of a place. It shows the place from above, like a bird sees it. A map cannot show everything. The person who makes it picks what to show. A bus map shows bus stops. People made maps long ago too. Someone in what is now Iraq made a map on clay. Sailors in the Marshall Islands made maps with sticks and shells. The shells showed islands.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Four tools help you read a map
read.sections.1.heading.source: Four tools help you read a map

read.sections.1.text.back: Most maps have four tools that help you read them. The title tells what the map is about. The legend, which is also called the key (keterangan), explains each symbol. A symbol is a colour, line or shape that stands for something real. On the Riverstone map, the blue line is the river, and the green square is the community centre. The compass shows directions, and sometimes it is only an arrow pointing north. The scale shows the ratio of distance on the map to the real distance. On this map, one square equals 100 metres, so the footpath that is four squares long is about 400 metres.
read.sections.1.text.source: Most maps include four tools that help you read them. The title tells you what the map is about. The key, which is also called a legend, explains each symbol. A symbol is a colour, line or shape that represents something real. On the Riverstone map, a blue line is the river, and a green square is the community centre. The compass rose shows directions, and sometimes it is simply an arrow pointing north. The scale shows how distance on the map compares with real distance. On this map, one square is 100 metres, so the four-square footpath is about 400 metres long.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Most maps have four tools. The title says what is in the map. The legend explains the meaning of each symbol. A symbol is a small shape, line or colour. A symbol stands for a real thing. On the Riverstone map, the blue line is the river. The compass shows north, south, east and west. The scale helps you know how far or near something is. Here, one square equals 100 metres. The footpath to the community centre is four squares long. So its length is about 400 metres.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Most maps have four tools. The title says what the map is about. The key tells what each symbol means. A symbol is a small shape, line or colour. It stands for a real thing. On the Riverstone map, a blue line is the river. The compass rose shows north, south, east and west. The scale helps you see how far things are. Here, one square is 100 metres. The path to the centre is four squares. So it is about 400 metres long.

read.sections.2.text.back: The footpath from East Housing is about 400 metres long, while the route by the main road is about 700 metres, so the footpath is the shorter route. But is it the best route for every visitor? The map does not tell whether the footpath is muddy, has steps, or has lights at night. The map also does not show whether the footbridge is open today. People who use that path every day know this information. A careful map reader uses the map as evidence, then asks local people who know that place. Maps are very useful, but a map is not the place itself.

People who use the path every day know this information. A careful map reader uses the map as evidence and then asks local people who know the place. A map is extremely useful, but it is not the place itself.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: The footpath via the bridge is 400 metres long. By the main road, the distance is 700 metres. So the footpath is the shorter route. But is it the best route? The map does not tell us everything. Is the path muddy? Are there steps? Is it dark at night? People who go there every day know. So look at the map first. Then ask people who know that place.

write.example.back: This map shows that the community centre is on the west side of the river. The footpath is about 400 metres long, and the route by the main road is about 700 metres. I would go via the footpath because it is shorter. Walk west from East Housing and cross the river by the footbridge. The community centre is the green square across the river. Before you go, I would ask the people who live near there whether the footpath has lights at night. I would also ask whether it has steps.

watch.summary.back: In this short video, the explorer Steve Backshall talks about map symbols. Ordnance Survey makes the maps of the United Kingdom. Every Ordnance Survey map has a legend, which is also called a key. The legend holds a list of symbols and the meaning of each symbol. A symbol is a small picture, line or colour. A symbol stands for a real thing, such as a footpath, a river or a building. Symbols save space, so a map can show many things in a small area. If you know the symbols, you can understand a place before going there. Maps from other map-makers might use different symbols. So always read the legend first.
watch.summary.source: In this short video, the explorer Steve Backshall talks about map symbols. Ordnance Survey makes maps of Great Britain. Every Ordnance Survey map has a key, which is also called a legend. The key lists the symbols and says what each one means. A symbol is a small picture, line or colour. It stands for a real thing, like a path, a river or a building. Symbols save space, so a map can show a lot in a small area. When you know the symbols, you can understand a place before you go there. Maps from other mapmakers may use different symbols. So always read the key first.
